# Stories and Visuals

Stories make data and numbers memorable. Stories are everywhere. When you think about the context of the data, stories evolve naturally: how does this data connect to you, your friends and family, your work, or society as a whole?

This chapter follows one data set from beginning to end — 87 dog breeds, each scored on intelligence, longevity, health, cost and grooming, and each ranked by how popular it is in the United States.[^stories-dogdata] By the end of the chapter the same numbers will have been shown as a sortable table, as a plain chart, as an award-winning poster, taken apart element by element, and finally used to settle an argument about whether we should be drawing bars at all.

```{r stories-setup, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

dogs_raw <- read.csv("data/Dogs/best_in_show.csv",
                     check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

dogs <- dogs_raw[-1, c(1, 3, 5, 6)]
names(dogs) <- c("Breed", "Group", "Score", "Popularity")
dogs <- dogs %>%
  mutate(Score = as.numeric(Score), Popularity = as.numeric(Popularity)) %>%
  filter(nzchar(trimws(Breed)), !is.na(Score), !is.na(Popularity))
```

## Facts versus visuals {#stories-facts}

A good story begins with facts, and facts usually arrive as a table. Here is the whole thing — all 87 breeds, nothing hidden, nothing summarised. **Click a column heading to sort it.**

```{r stories-dt, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
DT::datatable(
  dogs %>% select(Breed, Group,
                  `Data score` = Score,
                  `Popularity rank` = Popularity),
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(pageLength = 8, dom = "ftip",
                 columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-right", targets = 2:3))),
  caption = "All 87 breeds. Data score: higher is better, maximum 4.5. Popularity: 1 = most registered in the US.")
```

Now use it. *Which breed has the highest data score?* Sort the score column: **Border Collie**, 3.64. *Which is the most popular?* Sort the other one: **Labrador Retriever**, rank 1. Both answers are exact, both take two seconds, and no chart on earth would have given them to you faster.

This is worth saying plainly, because books like this one usually rush past it: **for looking a value up, and for ranking on one column, a table beats every chart.** If that is the question, do not draw anything.

### Where the table stops

Now a different question: **do Americans own the good dogs?**

That question is not about one column. It is about whether two columns move together. Sorting is still the right instinct — so sort by data score, and read *down the popularity column* beside it.

```{r stories-noise, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
by_score <- dogs %>% arrange(desc(Score))

set.seed(21)
z    <- as.numeric(scale(by_score$Score))
f    <- 0.35 * z + sqrt(1 - 0.35^2) * rnorm(nrow(by_score))
fake <- sort(by_score$Popularity)[rank(-f, ties.method = "first")]

tibble(Breed  = by_score$Breed,
       `Data score` = by_score$Score,
       `Popularity A` = by_score$Popularity,
       `Popularity B` = fake) %>%
  head(12) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Sorted by data score. One of the two popularity columns is the real one.",
               align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Read down column A: 45, 80, 30, 59, 130, 63, 27, 38, 60, 20. That is not an answer. That is a shrug.

But here is the problem, and it is worse than it looks. Column B is not real. It is the same 87 popularity values, reshuffled so that better dogs really *are* more popular — a correlation of −0.38, which in the social sciences is a strong finding, the kind of result a paper gets built around. Read down column B and try to see it. You may have a hunch. **A hunch is not a finding.**

A sorted table can tell you that a relationship is *not perfect*. It cannot tell you how strong it is, what shape it has, or which cases break it. And it fails silently: noise and a real effect produce columns that look the same.

This is what a chart is for. Not decoration, not persuasion. **A chart turns a reading problem into a seeing problem.**

```{r stories-ab, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=3.2, fig.cap="The same two columns, drawn. One second, not twelve rows."}
library(gridExtra)
ab <- function(y, ttl, col) {
  ggplot(data.frame(x = by_score$Score, y = y), aes(x, -y)) +
    geom_point(colour = col, size = 1.7) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = -c(1, 50, 100, 150), labels = c(1, 50, 100, 150)) +
    labs(title = ttl, x = "Data score", y = "Popularity rank") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}
grid.arrange(ab(by_score$Popularity, "A: r = 0.03", "grey45"),
             ab(fake, "B: r = -0.38", "#9b3f2d"), ncol = 2)
```

Nothing was added to the data between the table and the chart. Every number in the picture was already in the file. What changed is that the comparison moved from your patience into your eyes.

::: {.analysis-note}
Facts and visuals are not two different things. A visual **is** a fact, arranged so that a human can perceive it.

Which means a badly arranged visual is not merely ugly. It is a fact the reader cannot reach.
:::

## Telling a story {#stories-story}

From here on, panel A is the only real one. Let us look at it properly.

```{r stories-scatter, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=7, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="All 87 breeds at once. The grey lines mark the two averages, not zero."}
ms <- mean(dogs$Score); mp <- mean(dogs$Popularity)
hi <- dogs %>% filter(Breed %in% c("Border Collie", "Bulldog", "Labrador Retriever",
                                   "German Shepherd", "Border Terrier"))

ggplot(dogs, aes(Score, -Popularity)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = ms, xmax = 4.35, ymin = -mp, ymax = 5,
           fill = "#9b3f2d", alpha = .05) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -mp, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ms, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(colour = "grey55", size = 1.9) +
  geom_point(data = hi, colour = "#9b3f2d", size = 2.7) +
  geom_text(data = hi, aes(label = Breed), hjust = -0.13, size = 2.9,
            colour = "#9b3f2d") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.3, y = -18,  label = "popular AND good",
           hjust = 1, size = 2.9, fontface = "italic", colour = "grey35") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.62, y = -18, label = "popular but poor",
           hjust = 0, size = 2.9, fontface = "italic", colour = "grey35") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.3, y = -152, label = "good but overlooked",
           hjust = 1, size = 2.9, fontface = "italic", colour = "grey35") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.62, y = -152, label = "neither",
           hjust = 0, size = 2.9, fontface = "italic", colour = "grey35") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = -c(1, 50, 100, 150),
                     labels = c("1st", "50th", "100th", "150th")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.6, 4.35), ylim = c(-162, 3)) +
  labs(x = "Data score (higher = better dog, maximum 4.5)",
       y = "Popularity rank (1st = most owners)",
       title = "Popular dogs are not the best dogs",
       subtitle = "87 breeds. Grey lines mark the two averages, not zero.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8.5, colour = "grey35"))
```

The answer arrives in about one second, and it is **no**. The cloud does not run from bottom-left to top-right. If popularity tracked quality, it would.

### Reading the axes

Two things in that picture need explaining, and neither is obvious.

**The vertical axis is a rank, not a quantity.** It counts *positions*, not dogs. Rank 1 is the Labrador Retriever, rank 160 is somebody's beloved and very rare hound. The distance from rank 1 to rank 2 is not the same number of actual dogs as the distance from rank 100 to rank 101 — not remotely. A rank throws away the size of the gaps and keeps only the order. That is a real loss, and it is also why ranks are so common: they survive being merged from sources that measured different things.

Because a low number means *more* popular, the axis is drawn upside down, so that "up" means what a reader expects it to mean. Look at the tick labels: 1st at the top, 150th at the bottom.

**There is no origin.** A quantity has a meaningful zero — zero euros, zero students, zero grams. A rank does not. No dog has rank 0, and no dog has a data score of 0 either, because the score is built from percentile components that never bottom out. So the crossing lines cannot sit at (0, 0). They sit at the two **averages**: a data score of `r round(ms, 2)` and a popularity rank of `r round(mp, 1)`.

That choice has a consequence you should hold on to: the four regions are defined *relative to this set of 87 breeds*. Add fifty more breeds and the lines move.

:::: {.defbox}
::: {.titeldefbox}
<h2> The 2 × 2 matrix </h2>
:::
Cut two variables at one point each, and you get four boxes. Give the boxes names, and you have turned a cloud of points into an argument.

It is one of the most reused devices in all of analysis. The [BCG growth–share matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growth%E2%80%93share_matrix) splits market growth against market share and calls the corners *stars*, *cash cows*, *question marks*, *dogs* — genuinely, dogs. The Eisenhower matrix splits urgent against important. A **confusion matrix** splits what a model predicted against what was true, and its four boxes are the true positives, true negatives, false positives and false negatives on which every accuracy measure in this book is built. A 2 × 2 **contingency table** does the same for two yes/no variables.

The device is cheap and it is powerful, and it has one honest cost: **the cut is a decision**. A breed one hundredth of a point above the line gets a flattering name; the breed just below it does not. The names are a summary of the picture, never a substitute for it.
::::

```{r stories-corners, echo=FALSE}
dogs %>%
  mutate(Quadrant = case_when(
    Score >= ms & Popularity <= mp ~ "Popular and good",
    Score <  ms & Popularity <= mp ~ "Popular but poor",
    Score >= ms & Popularity >  mp ~ "Good but overlooked",
    TRUE                           ~ "Neither")) %>%
  count(Quadrant, name = "Breeds") %>%
  arrange(desc(Breeds)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Where the 87 breeds fall.", align = c("l", "r"))
```

### The story in the corners

The **Border Collie** has the highest data score of any breed, 3.64, and sits at rank 45 in popularity. The **Border Terrier** scores 3.61 and ranks 80th. Meanwhile the **Bulldog** is the sixth most popular dog in America with a score of 0.99 — the lowest of any breed people actually buy in numbers.

That is a story, and it did not come from a storyteller. It came from two columns and a scatterplot. Somebody who wanted to could now ask *why*: bulldogs are expensive, short-lived and prone to serious illness, and none of that stops people wanting one. Quality is not what makes a dog popular. Something else is.

### The designed version

The same data — the same file, in fact — was turned into a poster by David McCandless and *Information is Beautiful*.[^stories-iib]

```{r dogs, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align='center', fig.cap="*Best in Show: The Ultimate Data Dog*, by [Information is Beautiful](https://informationisbeautiful.net/visualizations/best-in-show-whats-the-top-data-dog/). The same 87 breeds as the scatterplot above."}
knitr::include_graphics("https://infobeautiful4.s3.amazonaws.com/2014/11/IIB_Best-In-Show_1276x2.png")
```

This is the takeaway of the section, so slow down and count what that poster is doing. It is the *same two-dimensional scatterplot* you just read — and it carries roughly ten variables in it:

| # | Variable | Visual channel |
|---:|:---|:---|
| 1 | Data score | horizontal position |
| 2 | Popularity rank | vertical position |
| 3 | Breed identity | the silhouette's shape |
| 4 | Kennel-club group | colour of the silhouette |
| 5 | Size category | size of the silhouette |
| 6 | Quadrant membership | which named region it falls in |
| 7 | Intelligence | folded into the score |
| 8 | Longevity | folded into the score |
| 9 | Genetic ailments | folded into the score |
| 10 | Cost and grooming | folded into the score |

A flat sheet of paper has exactly two dimensions. Everything past the second one has to be smuggled in through some other property of the mark: its shape, its colour, its size, its label, its position inside a named region. That is the whole craft. **Position is the strongest channel and you only get two of them — every further variable costs the reader something.**

And the corners are named: *Inexplicably Overrated*, *Hot Dogs!*, *The Rightly Ignored*, *Overlooked Treasures*. That naming does real work. It converts a statistical pattern into a claim somebody can argue with, which is exactly what a scatterplot on its own never manages.

::: {.analysis-note}
Notice what channels 7 to 10 cost. Four variables were compressed into one number before the drawing began, and the poster does not show you how.

The file does. The published score is exactly

`intelligence + longevity + ailments + 0.5 × (purchase price + food cost + grooming)`

with every component already converted to a percentile. For the Border Collie: 1.00 + 0.79 + 0.78 + 0.5 × (0.71 + 0.68 + 0.75) = **3.64**, the published figure. Reproducing all 87 scores this way agrees with the published column to within 0.015, which is just the rounding of the percentages.

So the weights are a *choice*: intelligence counts double what grooming counts. Change that one decision and the corners change breed. A reader of the poster cannot see this. A reader of the spreadsheet can.
:::

::: {.analysis-takeaway}
Design that makes a reader look longer is worth its ink. Design that makes a reader unable to check is not.

**Story before design. Design only where it helps understanding.**
:::

And somewhere in the poster there is a cat.

## Less is more {#stories-less}

Figure \@ref(fig:dogs) is a masterpiece of art and data science, and it is also the exception. It earns its complexity because it is a poster: something you stand in front of, in a museum or on a wall, and give five minutes to. Almost nothing you will make is a poster. A chart in a report, a slide, a paper or a dashboard gets a few seconds and must answer one question in them — and for that, everything the poster spends is a cost. From here on we go the other way: not how much can a graphic carry, but how little can it get away with.

Edward Tufte gave that principle a name.[^stories-tufte]
:::: {.defbox}
::: {.titeldefbox}
<h2> Definition </h2>
:::
The **data-ink ratio** is the proportion of the ink in a graphic that presents actual data, relative to the total ink used.

Tufte's prescription follows: show the data, maximise the data-ink ratio, erase non-data ink.
::::

Most charts fail this test not because anybody decided to clutter them, but because the software defaults did it for them. Below is one chart — the number of participants in seven terms of this course — taken apart one element at a time.

**Drag the slider, or click it and use the arrow keys.** Twenty-two steps. Nothing is ever added except at step 17.

```{r ink-slider, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, results='asis'}
counts <- read.csv(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MarcoKuehne/",
                          "marcokuehne.github.io/main/data/Course/GF_AllTime.csv"),
                   sep = ";") %>%
  count(Term, name = "Students")

# put the terms in calendar order, not alphabetical order
chrono <- c("SS 2020", "WS 2020 2021", "SS 2021", "SS 2022",
            "WS 2022 2023", "SS 2023", "WS 2023 2024")
counts <- counts[match(chrono, counts$Term), ]

short <- sub("^SS (\\d{4})$", "S\\1",
             sub("^WS (\\d{4}) \\d{4}$", "W\\1", counts$Term))

state <- list(frame = TRUE, plotbg = TRUE, panelbg = TRUE, minor = TRUE,
              gridcol = "black", vgrid = TRUE, hgrid = TRUE, border = TRUE,
              multicol = TRUE, legend = TRUE, xtitle = TRUE, bold = TRUE,
              ticks = TRUE, wide = TRUE, dark = TRUE, labels = FALSE,
              ytext = TRUE, ytitle = TRUE, axisline = TRUE,
              longnames = TRUE, rotate = TRUE)

draw <- function(s, caption) {
  d <- counts
  d$Lab <- factor(if (s$longnames) d$Term else short,
                  levels = if (s$longnames) d$Term else short)
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = Lab, y = Students))
  p <- p + if (s$multicol) {
    geom_col(aes(fill = Lab), colour = if (s$border) "black" else NA,
             linewidth = if (s$border) 1 else 0, width = if (s$wide) .9 else .65)
  } else {
    geom_col(fill = if (s$dark) "grey35" else "grey65",
             colour = if (s$border) "black" else NA,
             linewidth = if (s$border) 1 else 0, width = if (s$wide) .9 else .65)
  }
  if (s$labels) {
    p <- p + geom_text(aes(label = Students), vjust = -0.5, size = 3, colour = "grey20")
  }
  p + labs(title = "Course participants per term", subtitle = caption,
           x = if (s$xtitle) "Term" else NULL,
           y = if (s$ytitle) "Number of Students" else NULL) +
    theme_grey(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      plot.background = if (s$plotbg) {
        element_rect(fill = "grey95", colour = if (s$frame) "black" else NA,
                     linewidth = if (s$frame) 2 else 0)
      } else element_blank(),
      panel.background = if (s$panelbg) element_rect(fill = "grey80") else element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor = if (s$minor) element_line(colour = s$gridcol, linewidth = .3) else element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = if (s$vgrid) element_line(colour = s$gridcol, linewidth = .6) else element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = if (s$hgrid) element_line(colour = s$gridcol, linewidth = .6) else element_blank(),
      axis.line.y = if (s$axisline) element_line(colour = "grey40") else element_blank(),
      axis.ticks  = if (s$ticks) element_line() else element_blank(),
      axis.title  = if (s$bold) element_text(face = "bold") else element_text(),
      axis.text.y = if (s$ytext) element_text() else element_blank(),
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = if (s$rotate) 45 else 0,
                                 hjust = if (s$rotate) 1 else .5,
                                 face = if (s$bold) "bold" else "plain"),
      legend.position = if (s$legend) "right" else "none",
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8, colour = "grey30"))
}

steps <- list(
  c(NA,          "everything the defaults offer"),
  c("frame",     "outer frame removed"),
  c("plotbg",    "page background removed"),
  c("panelbg",   "panel background removed"),
  c("minor",     "minor gridlines removed"),
  c("gridcol",   "gridlines lightened"),
  c("vgrid",     "vertical gridlines removed - the bars already mark the categories"),
  c("hgrid",     "horizontal gridlines removed"),
  c("border",    "bar outlines removed"),
  c("multicol",  "colour removed - it encoded nothing the axis did not"),
  c("legend",    "legend removed - it repeated the axis labels"),
  c("xtitle",    "axis title removed - the labels already say it"),
  c("bold",      "bold removed"),
  c("ticks",     "tick marks removed"),
  c("wide",      "bars narrowed"),
  c("dark",      "fill lightened"),
  c("labels",    "numbers ADDED - ink spent to gain information"),
  c("ytext",     "y axis text removed - now redundant"),
  c("ytitle",    "y axis title removed"),
  c("axisline",  "axis line removed"),
  c("longnames", "labels shortened"),
  c("rotate",    "labels set horizontal"))

tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
s <- state
uris <- character(length(steps))
for (i in seq_along(steps)) {
  key <- steps[[i]][1]
  if (!is.na(key)) {
    s[[key]] <- if (key == "gridcol") "grey85" else if (key == "labels") TRUE else FALSE
  }
  ggsave(tmp, draw(s, sprintf("step %d of %d - %s", i, length(steps), steps[[i]][2])),
         width = 6, height = 3.8, dpi = 90, bg = "white")
  uris[i] <- knitr::image_uri(tmp)
}

cat('<div style="margin:1.5rem 0;">\n',
    '<img id="inkImg" src="', uris[1],
    '" alt="data-ink step" style="width:100%;border:1px solid #e3e3e3;border-radius:6px;">\n',
    '<input type="range" id="inkSlider" min="1" max="', length(steps),
    '" value="1" step="1" style="width:100%;margin-top:.6rem;">\n</div>\n',
    '<script>\nvar inkFrames = ["', paste(uris, collapse = '","'), '"];\n',
    '(function(){var i=document.getElementById("inkImg"),s=document.getElementById("inkSlider");',
    's.addEventListener("input",function(){i.src=inkFrames[+s.value-1];});})();\n</script>\n',
    sep = "")
```

Nothing was added between step 1 and step 22 except the numbers at step 17. Everything else was taken away: a frame, two background fills, two sets of gridlines, bar outlines, seven colours that encoded nothing, a legend that repeated the axis labels, an axis title, bold type, tick marks, and finally the y-axis itself.

:::: {.challenge}
::: {.titelchallenge}
<h2> Your Turn </h2>
:::
Drag back to step 1 and answer this: **which term had the most participants?** Now drag to step 22 and answer it again. Notice how long each took.

How many students were in that term? `r fitb(57)`

Step 17 is the only step that *adds* ink. Why is it still an improvement? `r mcq(c("It makes the chart look busier, which holds attention", answer = "It buys information — the exact values — and pays for the y-axis, which then becomes redundant", "It was a mistake in the sequence"))`

Everything else in those twenty-two steps was removed. Which removal cost the reader information? `r mcq(c("Removing the gridlines", "Removing the colour", answer = "None of them", "Removing the y-axis"))`

The bars stay in the order of the terms rather than being sorted from tallest to shortest. Why? `r mcq(c("It would look untidy", answer = "The terms have a natural order in time, and sorting would destroy it", "Sorting is always wrong"))`
::::

### What the ink is worth {#stories-ink}

Data-ink can be measured. Save each version as an image, count the pixels that are not white, and you have the ink the graphic actually spends.

| Step | | Ink (pixels) | Reduction |
|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | everything the defaults offer | 307,390 | — |
| 4 | backgrounds removed | 98,264 | 68 % |
| 11 | colour and legend removed | 99,825 | 68 % |
| 22 | data and labels only | 93,383 | **70 %** |

The final chart spends **70 % less ink and carries exactly the same seven numbers**. Two-thirds of the original was decoration, most of it gone in the first four steps. Note that step 11 uses slightly *more* ink than step 4 while looking cleaner — dropping the legend gave the panel more room, so the bars grew. Ink is a proxy, not a goal.

::: {.analysis-note}
Tufte was writing in 1983, about paper, when the metaphor was nearly literal. So take it literally.

A six-by-nine-inch page is about 0.035 m². Offset printing lays down an ink film of roughly one micrometre — around 1.2 grams per square metre at full coverage — and black offset ink costs on the order of ten to fifteen euros per kilogram. Replacing one bar chart with a leaner version saves about **0.0013 grams per copy**.

For a 500-copy academic monograph that is roughly **one cent**, for every chart in the book. For a 50,000-copy bestseller, under **one euro**.

These are order-of-magnitude estimates, and the direction is the point: **the data-ink ratio cannot be defended on economic grounds.** On paper it is worth cents. On a screen ink is free and the saving is exactly zero.
:::

So the principle must rest on something else, and it does. Non-data ink costs no money; it costs the reader's attention, which is the genuinely scarce resource. Every element competes for someone who will give the graphic a few seconds.

## Never use pie charts {#stories-pie}

That is about what a graphic spends. There is a second question: what the human eye can actually do.

The American Kennel Club sorts every breed into one of seven groups. Our 87 dogs divide up like this.

**Two questions. Which group has the most breeds? And are there more hounds or more toy breeds?**

```{r pie-chart, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=5.4, fig.height=4.2}
groups <- dogs %>%
  count(Group, name = "Breeds") %>%
  filter(nzchar(Group)) %>%
  arrange(Group)

par(mar = c(1, 1, 1, 1), xpd = TRUE)
pie(groups$Breeds, labels = groups$Group, radius = 0.86, cex = 0.9,
    col = grey(seq(.88, .58, length.out = nrow(groups))), border = "white")
```

Take a moment before you scroll.

<details>
<summary>**Can you tell now?**</summary>

```{r pie-bar, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=5.4, fig.height=3.4}
par(mar = c(6, 4, 1, 1), mgp = c(2.6, .6, 0))
barplot(groups$Breeds, names.arg = groups$Group, col = "grey65", border = NA,
        las = 2, cex.names = .85, ylab = "Breeds")
```

</details>

Sporting, with 15. And there are exactly as many hounds as toy breeds — 13 each. Both charts show the same seven numbers. The second answers both questions instantly; the first cannot answer either, and the tie is invisible in it. The reason is perceptual, not aesthetic: a pie asks you to compare **angles and areas**, a bar asks you to compare **positions along a common scale**.

Notice also what makes this example hard. The seven groups run from 10 to 15 breeds — shares of 11.5 % to 17.2 %. Nothing dominates. That is the ordinary case, and it is precisely the case a pie chart cannot serve.

Cleveland and McGill measured this. Position judgements were about **twice as accurate** as angle judgements, and **88 % of the large errors** occurred on the angle task.[^stories-cleveland]

R's own documentation is blunter. The help page for `pie()` states: *"Pie charts are a very bad way of displaying information."*

:::: {.amazing}
::: {.titelamazing}
<h2> When a pie chart is defensible </h2>
:::
Two or three slices, one obviously dominant, and the point being *part of a whole* rather than a comparison between parts.

Recent work is gentler than the folklore: pies, donuts and bars performed **equally well for extracting part–whole relationships**, and the differences that appeared were often small. Bars won on *ranking* and were faster overall.[^stories-hill]

The rule is not "pie charts are evil." It is: **the moment a reader has to rank the slices, use bars.**
::::

## Then why use bars at all? {#stories-bars}

Follow the argument to its end and it turns on the bar chart itself. A bar spends a lot of ink to place one number: a filled rectangle from zero to the value, when only the *tip* carries information. If position along a scale is what the eye reads well, a dot at the same height would do the same job.

```{r stories-dotplot, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=3, fig.cap="The ten best-scoring breeds, twice. The dots carry the same information."}
library(gridExtra)
top <- dogs %>% arrange(desc(Score)) %>% head(10) %>%
  mutate(Breed = factor(Breed, levels = rev(Breed)))

pa <- ggplot(top, aes(Score, Breed)) + geom_col(fill = "grey60") +
  labs(title = "Bar chart", x = "Data score", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
pb <- ggplot(top, aes(Score, Breed)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = Score, yend = Breed), colour = "grey85", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, colour = "grey25") +
  labs(title = "Dot plot", x = "Data score", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

grid.arrange(pa, pb, ncol = 2)
```

That is Cleveland's **dot plot**.[^stories-dotplot] Ten breeds, ten numbers, a fraction of the ink — and nothing lost.

Meanwhile a survey of 703 physiology papers found **85.6 % contained at least one bar graph**.[^stories-weissgerber]

So: technically we could plot almost anything. Empirically, people plot bars. What lies between? Three things are worth keeping before you delete every bar you own.

**Bars carry the zero.** A dot plot frees you from the baseline — which is exactly the risk. Truncating an axis biases judgement in any encoding, even when the truncation is visibly marked.[^stories-truncation]

```{r stories-zero, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=2.6, fig.cap="Same five breeds, same scores, two axes."}
sel <- dogs %>% arrange(desc(Score)) %>% head(5) %>%
  mutate(Breed = factor(Breed, levels = rev(Breed)))

pz <- ggplot(sel, aes(Score, Breed)) + geom_col(fill = "grey60") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 3.8)) +
  labs(title = "Zero baseline: the breeds are nearly equal", x = "Data score", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
pt <- ggplot(sel, aes(Score, Breed)) + geom_col(fill = "#9b3f2d") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(3.3, 3.7)) +
  labs(title = "Truncated: a dramatic ranking appears", x = "Data score", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

grid.arrange(pz, pt, ncol = 2)
```

**Bars mean "compare these separate things."** Readers reliably associate bars with discrete comparisons and lines with trends, without ever being taught to.[^stories-zacks] That association is not decoration — it is a claim about the data, and the wrong mark makes a claim the data cannot support.

Here are the seven kennel-club groups again, drawn three ways.

```{r stories-barsline, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=9, fig.height=3, fig.cap="The same seven numbers. Only the middle and right panels disagree with each other."}
o1 <- c("herding", "hound", "non-sporting", "sporting", "terrier", "toy", "working")
o2 <- c("toy", "terrier", "herding", "non-sporting", "hound", "working", "sporting")

mk <- function(ord, type, ttl) {
  dd <- groups %>% mutate(Group = factor(Group, levels = ord)) %>% arrange(Group)
  p  <- ggplot(dd, aes(Group, Breeds, group = 1))
  p  <- if (type == "bar") p + geom_col(fill = "grey60") else
    p + geom_line(colour = "#9b3f2d", linewidth = .9) +
        geom_point(colour = "#9b3f2d", size = 2)
  p + labs(title = ttl, x = NULL, y = "Breeds") +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 16)) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 8.5) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

grid.arrange(mk(o1, "bar",  "Bars, alphabetical order"),
             mk(o1, "line", "A line through the same numbers"),
             mk(o2, "line", "The same line, categories reordered"), ncol = 3)
```

The middle panel invents a story: a dip at *non-sporting*, a peak at *sporting*, a recovery. The right-hand panel tells a completely different story — a steady climb — and it is the *same seven numbers*. Only the order of the categories changed, and the order of the categories is arbitrary, because "toy" does not come before or after "hound" in any sense the world cares about.

A line asserts that the space *between* two points means something. Between "terrier" and "toy" there is nothing. The bars survive reordering because they never made that claim; the line does not, because it did. This is why the seven terms of the course stay bars: a bar says *these are seven separate cohorts*, not one continuous quantity that existed in between.

**Familiarity is real, and small.** The conventional vertical bar is identified faster than horizontal bars or lines — by roughly 35 to 55 milliseconds.[^stories-typicality]

```{r stories-orientation, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Breeds per kennel-club group. The vertical version is recognised faster; the horizontal version reads its labels more easily."}
g <- dogs %>% count(Group, name = "n") %>% filter(nzchar(Group))

pv <- ggplot(g, aes(reorder(Group, -n), n)) + geom_col(fill = "grey60") +
  labs(title = "Vertical: identified in ~720 ms", x = NULL, y = "Breeds") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
ph <- ggplot(g, aes(n, reorder(Group, n))) + geom_col(fill = "grey60") +
  labs(title = "Horizontal: ~757 ms, but labels stay level", x = "Breeds", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

grid.arrange(pv, ph, ncol = 2)
```

That is an advantage in *recognition speed*, not in accuracy of reading values — and the horizontal version buys something back, since its labels do not have to be tilted.

::: {.analysis-takeaway}
**Technically possible:** almost any encoding, animated, interactive, three-dimensional.

**Actually used:** bars and pies, because that is what spreadsheets offer. Across 42,000 web charts, the bar share ranged from 12 % to 57 % depending only on *which tool* made them.[^stories-usage]

**The defensible middle:** the most conventional form that supports the judgement your reader must make. Bars for separate categories with a meaningful zero. Dots when zero is not meaningful, labels are long, or many series compete. Lines for trends.

And spend what you saved on the thing that helps most: **put the message in the title** and label the data directly, so nobody has to translate a legend before they can think.
:::

:::: {.challenge}
::: {.titelchallenge}
<h2> Your Turn </h2>
:::
Here is the participants-per-term chart once more, as bars and as dots, so you do not have to scroll back.

```{r stories-terms-two, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=8, fig.height=2.6, fig.cap="Course participants per term, two ways."}
ct <- counts %>% mutate(Term = factor(Term, levels = Term))

tb <- ggplot(ct, aes(Term, Students)) + geom_col(fill = "grey60") +
  labs(title = "Bars", x = NULL, y = "Students") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8.5) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
td <- ggplot(ct, aes(Term, Students)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, colour = "grey25") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(title = "Dots", x = NULL, y = "Students") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8.5) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

grid.arrange(tb, td, ncol = 2)
```

Would the dot plot be the better choice here? `r mcq(c("Yes, less ink is always better", answer = "No — these are separate cohorts and zero students is a meaningful floor, so the bars earn their ink", "It makes no difference"))`

Now the harder half of the same question. For the ten dog breeds a few figures earlier, the dot plot *was* the better choice. What is different about that case? `r mcq(c("There were more categories", answer = "No breed can score zero, so the bars measured from a baseline that does not exist", "Dogs are not students"))`

The scatterplot at the start of this chapter is titled "Popular dogs are not the best dogs." Change it to "Data score against popularity rank" and look again. Which change altered the graphic more — the twenty-two removals, or the title?

[^stories-dogdata]: *Best in Show: The Ultimate Data Dog*, data compiled by Information is Beautiful from American Kennel Club registrations and other sources: <https://informationisbeautiful.net/visualizations/best-in-show-whats-the-top-data-dog/>. The file used here is `data/Dogs/best_in_show.csv`; 87 of 174 breeds carry both a data score and a popularity rank.

[^stories-iib]: McCandless, D., *Best in Show: The Ultimate Data Dog*, Information is Beautiful, <https://informationisbeautiful.net/visualizations/best-in-show-whats-the-top-data-dog/>.

[^stories-tufte]: Tufte, E. R., *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, 2nd edition, Graphics Press, 2001 (first edition 1983). The data-ink ratio is developed in Chapter 4.

[^stories-cleveland]: Cleveland, W. S., and McGill, R., *Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods*, *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 79(387), 1984, 531--554, <https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478080>. Their own ranking leaves length, direction and angle tied; the familiar tie-free ordering is Mackinlay's adaptation, *ACM Transactions on Graphics* 5(2), 1986, 110--141.

[^stories-hill]: Hill, A., *Are pie charts evil? An assessment of the value of pie and donut charts compared to bar charts*, *Information Visualization*, 2025, <https://doi.org/10.1177/14738716241259432>.

[^stories-dotplot]: Cleveland, W. S., *Graphical Methods for Data Presentation: Full Scale Breaks, Dot Charts, and Multibased Logging*, *The American Statistician* 38(4), 1984, 270--280. Developed further in *The Elements of Graphing Data*, Wadsworth, 1985.

[^stories-weissgerber]: Weissgerber, T. L., Milic, N. M., Winham, S. J., and Garovic, V. D., *Beyond Bar and Line Graphs: Time for a New Data Presentation Paradigm*, *PLOS Biology* 13(4), 2015, e1002128. Survey of 703 articles in the top quartile of physiology journals.

[^stories-truncation]: Correll, M., Bertini, E., and Franconeri, S., *Truncating the Y-Axis: Threat or Menace?*, *Proceedings of CHI 2020*, <https://doi.org/10.1145/3313831.3376222>.

[^stories-zacks]: Zacks, J., and Tversky, B., *Bars and lines: A study of graphic communication*, *Memory & Cognition* 27(6), 1999, 1073--1079.

[^stories-typicality]: Reimann, D., Struwe, M., Ram, N., and Gaschler, R., *Typicality effect in data graphs*, *Visual Communication* 24(1), 2025, 114--128. Vertical bars were identified in about 720 ms, horizontal bars 757 ms, lines 773 ms.

[^stories-usage]: Battle, L., Duan, P., Miranda, Z., Mukusheva, D., Chang, R., and Stonebraker, M., *Beagle: Automated Extraction and Interpretation of Visualizations from the Web*, *Proceedings of CHI 2018*. Over 42,000 charts; bar, line, scatter and map account for 65 % to 90 % of each collection.
